mechanisms.name: Internal gear pair
mechanisms.summary: A pinion meshes inside a ring with teeth on its inner rim, so both turn the same way on close, parallel shafts.

ratio.typical: 1.5:1 to 5:1 per pair; default 40/18 = 2.22:1

topology.notes: ground, pinion, internal gear; one internal gear mesh

explain.motion: The 18-tooth pinion rolls inside a 40-tooth internal gear. Because the teeth meet on the same side of both centres, ring and pinion turn in the same direction, the ring at 18/40 of the pinion speed.
explain.forces: A concave ring tooth wraps around a convex pinion tooth, so contact stress is lower and more teeth share the load than in an external pair. The radial separating force acts toward the ring centre and is taken by both bearings.
explain.benefits: Very short centre distance (half the tooth-count difference times the module), same-direction rotation without an idler, and a natural housing for planetary sets.
explain.limits: Too small a tooth difference causes tip and trochoid interference, so standard 20° gears need about 10 or more teeth difference and more than 34 ring teeth. Internal teeth must be shaped or broached rather than hobbed, which costs more.

mechanisms.name: Rack-and-pinion stroke doubler
mechanisms.summary: A pinion carried on a slide rolls on a fixed rack and drives a free rack on its far side twice as far as the slide moves.

ratio.typical: output stroke = 2 x carrier stroke for any pinion; 160 mm for an 80 mm carrier stroke

topology.notes: ground with the fixed rack, carrier (prismatic on the ground), pinion (revolute on the carrier), free rack (prismatic on the ground); two gear meshes, the pinion with each rack

explain.motion: A carrier slides back and forth with a pinion turning on its axle. The pinion meshes a fixed rack on one side and a free rack on the other. As the carrier moves, the pinion rolls along the fixed rack, so its contact there stands still for an instant: it is the instant centre. The far side of the pitch circle is twice as far from that point as the axle, so it moves twice as fast: the free rack moves 160 mm while the carrier moves 80 mm, the same way, whatever the pinion's size.
explain.forces: The free rack's load comes back through the pinion on both sides: the carrier pushes with twice the output force, half of it taken by the fixed rack, so the stroke doubles and the force halves. The pressure angle of each mesh pushes the racks away from the pinion, and their guides take it.
explain.benefits: Doubles a short stroke in a narrow space with an exact, positive drive, and the 2:1 holds for any pinion, since only the rolling sets it.
explain.limits: The backlash of two meshes adds up at the output, and the racks must stay parallel over the whole stroke or the pinion binds. The carrier needs twice the output force, and the ratio cannot be changed.

build.ground: base with the fixed rack screwed and dowelled to it, a slide for the carrier and a slide for the free rack, all along x
build.defining_relations: The pinion (module 3, 16 teeth, pitch radius r = 24 mm) rolls on the fixed rack's pitch line: for a carrier travel x it turns θ = -x / r. The free rack meshes it on the opposite side, 2r from the fixed pitch line, and moves x - r θ = 2x, whatever r is. Carrier stroke 80 mm (±40), free rack stroke 160 mm (±80), pinion turn 191° over the stroke (80 / 24 rad).
build.notes: Seen in plan: the fixed rack below the pinion's centre, teeth up, the free rack above, teeth down. Relative to the carrier each rack moves ±40 mm, so 16 teeth (150.8 mm) keep both in mesh over the stroke. The carrier is the driven slide; the free rack rides its own slide from its back, its toothed side open for the pinion.

review.note: New record (#257), reviewed against its kinematics before the build and again on the six phases of the finished build. Six phases (every 60 degrees of the cycle): the carrier at -40, -20, +20, +40, +20, -20 mm and the free rack at -80, -40, +40, +80, +40, -40 mm, always twice the carrier and the same way; the pinion turns back as it rolls forward, +95.5 to -95.5 degrees (191 over the stroke, 80 / 24 rad); its contact with the fixed rack stays on the fixed pitch line under the axle. Decided: the carrier is driven by the linear drive along its own slide (standard section 8), not by Brown's crank and rod, so the lesson is the two straight strokes alone with no second mechanism in front of it; module 3, 16 teeth (pitch radius 24), a carrier stroke of 80 mm and a free rack stroke of 160 mm; both racks 16 teeth, enough to stay in mesh over the stroke; the carrier 84 mm long, so it shows past the pinion at both ends; the fixed rack drawn as frame (role frame) and the free rack as the output, so which rack moves reads at a glance. Default view PLAN (opened at 28 degrees), where the pitch circle, both pitch lines and both strokes show true. Traces: a mark on the free rack's pitch line (the comet) and the axle, both ticked every 30 degrees of the cycle, so at every tick the rack's step is twice the carrier's; overlays: the fixed pitch line, a circle at the instant centre, the line from it through the axle to the far contact (speeds 0, v, 2v), and the two stroke dimensions between the posed ends. Plot of the free rack against the carrier (a straight line of slope 2). Controls: the input only; the pinion size is not offered (the parts are built for one pinion), and the claim that the ratio holds for any pinion is the law, checked by the block's test at three radii. mechanisms.name: Sun and planet gear
mechanisms.summary: A planet gear fixed to a beam engine's connecting rod orbits a sun gear on the flywheel shaft, turning the shaft twice per orbit.

ratio.typical: shaft turns = 1 + zp/zs per planet orbit; 2 turns per beam double stroke with equal gears

topology.notes: ground, beam, connecting rod with planet rigidly fixed, sun with flywheel, retaining link from sun shaft to planet centre; one gear mesh

explain.motion: The beam rocks and drives the connecting rod, whose lower end carries a planet gear that cannot turn relative to the rod. A retaining link keeps the planet in mesh as its centre orbits the sun gear on the flywheel shaft. Because the planet does not spin on its own axis, the sun is driven round by both the orbit and the rolling mesh, so with equal gears the shaft makes two turns per orbit. The rod tilts as it moves, so the sun's speed swings between 1.68 and 2.33 times the orbit speed.
explain.forces: The rod thrust acts at the mesh, tangential to the sun, so torque is the rod force times the pitch radius of the sun, varying with rod angle like a crank. The retaining link carries the radial separating force; the gear teeth and the link pivot are the weak points under shock.
explain.benefits: Gets rotary output from a reciprocating beam without a crank and doubles shaft speed compared with a crank. It has no dead centre in the way a single crank does at top and bottom.
explain.limits: More parts, gear wear and backlash than a simple crank, and the flywheel is still needed to smooth the torque. It fell out of use once the crank patent expired around 1794.

mechanisms.name: Worm drive
mechanisms.summary: A screw-like worm turns a toothed wheel on a crossing shaft, giving a large reduction in one stage that often cannot be driven backwards.

ratio.typical: 5:1 to 75:1 per stage (up to about 100:1); ratio = wheel teeth / worm starts; default 30:1

topology.notes: ground, worm, wheel; one worm mesh (screw-type sliding contact)

explain.motion: The worm is a screw with one thread (start). Each worm turn advances the wheel by one tooth, so a 30-tooth wheel turns once per 30 worm turns. The shafts cross at 90° without intersecting.
explain.forces: Contact is mostly sliding along the thread, so friction is high and efficiency falls from about 90% at low ratios to under 50% at high ratios. The drive locks when the lead angle is below the friction angle: here the lead angle is 5.7°, and at rest steel on bronze has a friction coefficient of about 0.12 (friction angle about 7.3°), so the wheel cannot turn the worm. Running, the coefficient falls to about 0.06 (3.7°), which is why the lock is not reliable under vibration.
explain.benefits: Very high reduction in one compact, quiet stage, and a self-locking worm holds loads without a brake in many uses.
explain.limits: Low efficiency and heat build-up; a steel worm needs a bronze wheel and good lubrication. Self-locking is unreliable under vibration, so it should not replace a safety brake on hoists.

mechanisms.name: Crossed helical gears
mechanisms.summary: Two helical gears on non-parallel, non-intersecting shafts touch at a point and drive each other, usually at 90°, for light loads.

ratio.typical: 1:1 to about 5:1; ratio = z2/z1 (not pitch diameter ratio); default 24/12 = 2:1

topology.notes: ground, gear 1, gear 2; one point-contact crossed helical mesh

explain.motion: Two ordinary helical gears of the same hand are mounted on shafts crossing at 90° at a set distance, without meeting. With 45° helix angles the teeth line up at the contact and gear 1 (12 teeth) turns gear 2 (24 teeth) at half speed. Changing how the shaft angle is split between the two helix angles changes both diameters and the centre distance, but not the ratio: that is set by the tooth counts alone.
explain.forces: Contact is a single point that slides along the teeth, so load capacity is low and wear is high. Each gear sees an axial thrust that must be taken by its bearings.
explain.benefits: Lets two standard helical gears drive between skew shafts, and centre distance and ratio can be tuned by choosing different helix angles. Insensitive to small centre-distance errors.
explain.limits: Point contact and high sliding limit them to light power, such as camshaft-driven distributors and oil pumps; for real loads use a worm or hypoid set.

mechanisms.name: Cycloidal drive
mechanisms.summary: An eccentric drives a lobed disc around a ring of pins; one fewer lobe than pins gives a large, compact, shock-tolerant reduction.

ratio.typical: about 9:1 to 100:1 per stage; ratio = n / (N - n); default 9:1

topology.notes: ground with 10 ring pins, eccentric input shaft, cycloidal disc, output flange with pins; higher pairs: disc lobes on ring pins (rolling, all ten counted as one), output pins in disc holes (pin-in-hole, all six counted as one)

explain.motion: The input shaft carries an eccentric that makes the cycloidal disc wobble around inside a ring of 10 fixed pins. Because the disc has 9 lobes, one fewer than the pins, it rolls backwards by one lobe, 40°, for every input turn, so the output turns once, backwards, per 9 input turns (9:1). Pins on the output flange run in holes in the disc whose radius exceeds the pin's by the eccentricity: each hole circles its pin, so the wobble is left behind and only the slow turn reaches the flange.
explain.forces: Many lobes touch ring pins at once (in theory about half), so load is shared and the drive survives shock loads well. The eccentric disc creates an unbalanced force, so real units use two discs 180° apart.
explain.benefits: High ratio in one compact stage, rolling contact with high efficiency (often above 90%), high shock tolerance and low backlash.
explain.limits: Single discs vibrate unless balanced, the profile must be made precisely, and output torque has a small ripple. More parts than a planetary stage.

mechanisms.name: Differential
mechanisms.summary: Splits one input between two output shafts so they can turn at different speeds, their average always equal to the carrier speed.

ratio.typical: final drive 2.5:1 to 5:1 into the case; 1:1 average to the two side shafts; default 41/10 = 4.1:1

topology.notes: ground, input pinion, ring gear and case (one body), two spider pinions, left and right side gears; meshes: pinion-ring and each spider with both side gears. Overconstrained: the second spider is redundant (a body, a pin and two meshes, net -1 in the count), so the count gives 1 against the true mobility 2: the case speed and the side gears' speed difference.

explain.motion: The input pinion turns the ring gear and the case it is fixed to, at 10/41 of the pinion speed. Two spider pinions on a cross-pin in the case mesh with both side gears. When the side gears turn at the case speed the spiders do not spin on their pin and the whole set turns as one. When one side gear runs ahead of the case, the spiders spin and the other side gear falls behind by the same amount, so the average of the two side gears is always the case speed. Hold one side gear and the other turns at twice the case speed.
explain.forces: An open differential always gives equal torque to both outputs, so the wheel with least grip limits total traction. The spider pinions only carry load across their own teeth and turn only when the wheels differ in speed.
explain.benefits: Lets driven wheels on one axle cover different distances in a turn without scrubbing tyres, and as a mechanism it adds or averages two rotations exactly.
explain.limits: If one wheel loses grip it spins and the other gets almost no torque; limited-slip or locking differentials address this at the cost of complexity.

mechanisms.name: Harmonic drive
mechanisms.summary: An elliptical wave generator flexes a thin toothed cup inside a rigid ring with two more teeth, giving a 50:1 to 160:1 coaxial reduction with no backlash.

ratio.typical: 30:1 to 160:1 per stage; ratio = Zf / (Zc - Zf); drawn with coarse teeth at 30/2 = 15:1, and 100/2 = 50:1 as the alternative tooth set

topology.notes: ground with circular spline, wave generator, flexspline (compliant); one multi-tooth mesh at two zones. The wave generator bearing sets the flexspline's shape, not its angle, so it is not counted as a rigid pair in the mobility (the flexure block carries it).

explain.motion: An elliptical cam with a thin ball bearing (the wave generator) spins inside a flexible cup with 30 external teeth (the flexspline), bending it into an oval so its teeth engage a rigid 32-tooth ring at the two ends of the long axis and stand clear at the ends of the short one. Each wave generator turn shifts the flexspline back by two teeth relative to the ring, 24°, so the flexspline turns once, backwards, per 15 input turns (15:1). With the finer 100 and 102 teeth of the other tooth set the reduction is 50:1, but the bend is then too small to see.
explain.forces: About 30% of the teeth are in contact at once, giving high torque capacity and stiffness for the size. The flexspline is cyclically bent every half turn, so its fatigue strength sets the torque and life limits.
explain.benefits: High single-stage ratio, near-zero backlash, coaxial hollow-shaft design and light weight make it the standard robot joint reducer.
explain.limits: Torsional compliance is higher than in rigid gears, the flexspline can fail by fatigue or ratcheting under overload, and efficiency falls at high ratios and low temperatures.

mechanisms.name: Hypoid gear pair
mechanisms.summary: A spiral bevel pair with the pinion axis offset below the gear centre, so the shafts cross without meeting; used in car rear axles.

ratio.typical: 2.5:1 to 5:1 in car axles, up to about 10:1; default 41/10 = 4.1:1

topology.notes: ground, pinion, ring gear; one hypoid mesh with sliding along the tooth

explain.motion: The 10-tooth pinion drives a 41-tooth ring gear through 90° (4.1:1), but its axis passes 25 mm to one side of the ring gear's axis, so the two shafts cross without meeting. To mesh at that offset the pinion has a larger spiral angle than the gear, which makes it larger and stronger than a spiral bevel pinion of the same ratio, here about a third larger across.
explain.forces: The offset adds sliding along the teeth, so tooth friction is higher than in a bevel pair and extreme-pressure hypoid oil is required. Contact is spread over several curved teeth at once, giving high load capacity and smooth, quiet running.
explain.benefits: The lowered pinion lets a car's propeller shaft sit lower (less floor tunnel), and the bigger pinion and higher contact ratio carry more torque quietly.
explain.limits: Efficiency (about 90 to 96%) is lower than bevel gears, requires special lubricant, and setup of pinion depth and backlash is critical. Manufacturing needs dedicated Gleason or Klingelnberg type machines.

mechanisms.name: Non-circular gears
mechanisms.summary: Gears with non-round pitch curves, such as a pair of ellipses turning on their foci, give a speed ratio that varies through each turn.

ratio.typical: ratio swings between (1-e)/(1+e) and (1+e)/(1-e) each turn; 1/3 to 3 at e = 0.5

topology.notes: ground, gear 1, gear 2; one non-circular gear mesh

explain.motion: Two identical elliptical gears each turn about one focus, with the foci 80 mm apart (the major axis length). The contact point always lies on the line of centres and runs 40 mm each way along it, so the two radii to it trade length while their sum stays the same, and the speed ratio is their quotient. As the driver turns steadily, the driven gear turns the other way, speeding up and slowing down once per turn, from a third of the input speed to three times it: in the 120° of input around the meeting of the long radius with the short one it turns 240°.
explain.forces: Torque transmitted scales inversely with the instantaneous speed ratio, so the driven shaft sees cyclic torque and the system sees inertia loads from the varying speed. Pressure angle varies along the profile, which limits the eccentricity before teeth jam or undercut.
explain.benefits: Produces an exact, repeatable non-uniform motion with continuous rotation, useful for quick-return strokes, matching cutter speed to web speed, or oval-gear flow metering.
explain.limits: Hard to design and manufacture (each tooth differs), noisier than round gears, and large eccentricity causes undercut and interference. Cams or linkages are often cheaper for one-off motion laws.

mechanisms.name: Planetary gear set
mechanisms.summary: Planets orbit a central sun inside a ring gear; hold the ring, drive the sun, and the carrier turns slowly in line with the input.

ratio.typical: 3:1 to 10:1 per stage with ring fixed; default 1 + 35/13 = 3.69:1

topology.notes: ground, ring, sun, carrier, 3 planets; sun, ring and carrier revolute to ground, each planet revolute on the carrier; 3 sun-planet and 3 planet-ring meshes. Overconstrained: two of the three planets are redundant (each adds a body, a pin and two meshes, net -1 in the count), so the count gives 0 against the true mobility 2 with the ring free; with the ring held it is 1.

explain.motion: The sun drives three planets, which roll around inside the fixed ring and carry the carrier with them. With 13 sun teeth and a 35-tooth ring, the carrier turns once for every 1 + 35/13 = 3.69 turns of the sun, in the same direction, while each planet spins backwards on its own pin.
explain.forces: Load is shared between three planets, so each mesh carries about a third of the torque and the radial pushes on the sun cancel. The ring reacts the difference between input and output torque.
explain.benefits: Coaxial input and output, very high torque density, and by choosing which of sun, ring or carrier is held, the same parts give different ratios; with two inputs it adds or subtracts speeds.
explain.limits: Tooth counts are constrained by assembly and spacing rules, load sharing needs accurate parts or floating members, and the many meshes make it costlier than a simple pair.

mechanisms.name: Ravigneaux planetary gearset
mechanisms.summary: Two suns, short and long pinions on one carrier and a single ring give several forward ratios and reverse in a compact automatic gearbox.

ratio.typical: with defaults: 1st 2.80:1, 2nd 1.54:1, 3rd 1:1, reverse -2.33:1

topology.notes: ground, small sun, large sun, carrier, ring, three short and three long pinions; per pinion set the meshes small sun-short, short-long, long-large sun and long-ring. Overconstrained: the second and third pinion sets are redundant (each adds 2 bodies, 2 pins and 4 meshes, net -2 in the count), so the count gives -2 against the true mobility 2; the gear selector holds or locks a member to leave 1.

explain.motion: Short pinions mesh with the small sun and with the long pinions; long pinions mesh with the large sun and the ring. All pinions ride on one carrier, so the set has two degrees of freedom: drive one member, hold another, and the ratio is fixed. In 1st the carrier is held and the small sun drives the ring at 30/84, a 2.80:1 reduction. In 2nd the large sun is held: the carrier turns at 0.455 of the input, the pinions orbit and spin, and the ring turns at 0.649, 1.54:1. In 3rd two members are locked together and the whole set turns as one, 1:1. In reverse the carrier is held and the large sun drives: the ring turns backwards at 36/84, 2.33:1.
explain.forces: Torque splits between three pinion pairs, so tooth loads are shared and the unit carries high torque for its size. The held member's brake takes the reaction torque; the short-to-long pinion meshes see the highest tooth loads in low gear.
explain.benefits: Gives three or four forward speeds and reverse from one compact coaxial gearset with fewer parts than two simple planetaries.
explain.limits: Ratio spacing is constrained by shared tooth counts, and the long pinions and their bearings are a weak point. Shifts need coordinated clutch and brake timing.

mechanisms.name: Wankel rotary engine
mechanisms.summary: A triangular rotor orbits inside an epitrochoid housing, phased by a 3:2 internal gear, turning the eccentric shaft three times per rotor turn.

ratio.typical: eccentric shaft 3 turns per rotor turn (rotor gear : fixed gear = 3:2)

topology.notes: ground (housing with fixed external gear), eccentric shaft, rotor with internal gear; one gear mesh; apex seals sliding on the housing are redundant contacts

explain.motion: The rotor's internal gear rolls on a fixed gear on the housing, so the rotor centre orbits the shaft axis on the eccentric while the rotor turns slowly the same way. Its three apexes stay on the epitrochoid wall, forming three chambers that grow and shrink twice per rotor turn. The eccentric shaft turns three times for each rotor revolution, giving one power stroke per shaft turn per rotor.
explain.forces: Gas pressure on each rotor flank pushes through the rotor bearing onto the eccentric, producing torque equal to force times eccentricity. The phasing gears carry only the reaction that keeps the rotor in step, while apex seals take sliding contact loads and wear.
explain.benefits: Very compact and smooth for its power, with no reciprocating parts and few moving pieces.
explain.limits: Long thin combustion chambers burn poorly, giving higher fuel use and emissions. Apex seal wear and oil consumption limit life.

mechanisms.name: Star wheel and pin
mechanisms.summary: A finger on a turning shaft knocks a star wheel on by one tooth per turn, and a sprung jumper snaps it into place and holds it.

ratio.typical: 36° per driver turn (10 teeth); 31 teeth for a date wheel

topology.notes: ground, driver with finger pin, star wheel, jumper lever with roller; finger-star and jumper-star contacts; jumper spring

explain.motion: A driver turns continuously and once per turn its finger enters a gap of the star wheel and pushes one tooth. A spring-loaded jumper rides up the flank of the next tooth. At the crest, 18° into the step, the jumper takes over: it snaps the star on into the next gap, 36° in all, over 8° of driver, while the finger turns out of the gap. Between steps the jumper holds the star still.
explain.forces: The finger works against the jumper spring until the tooth tip passes, then the spring does the last part of the step. The finger load is light but the snap gives a small impact and holding force depends entirely on the spring.
explain.benefits: Very simple, cheap and compact, with a crisp, well-defined rest position. The output can step through any number of positions per revolution.
explain.limits: Holding is only spring force, so it suits light loads and slow rates. Backdriving with enough force can jump the jumper.

mechanisms.name: Geneva drive
mechanisms.summary: A pin on a constantly turning crank enters a slot and steps a slotted wheel a quarter turn, then a locking disc holds it still.

ratio.typical: 90° per index (4-slot), moving for 90° of crank, dwell 270°

topology.notes: ground, crank (arm with pin and locking disc), slotted wheel; pin-in-slot and locking arc contact alternate, so only one acts at a time; counted mobility 0 with both declared

explain.motion: The crank turns continuously; its pin enters a slot tangentially, drives the wheel through a quarter turn and leaves tangentially. While the pin is out, a raised locking disc on the crank sits in a concave arc on the wheel and holds it still. With 4 slots the wheel moves during 90° of crank rotation and rests for 270°.
explain.forces: The pin pushes on the slot wall; torque on the wheel is highest mid-index when the pin is closest to the wheel centre. Acceleration jumps at entry and exit, so impact and wear grow quickly with speed.
explain.benefits: Positive indexing and locking with very few parts, and the entry and exit have zero wheel velocity.
explain.limits: Infinite jerk at entry and exit limits speed, and the index angle is fixed by the slot count. The ratio of motion to dwell cannot be chosen freely.

mechanisms.name: Intermittent gear
mechanisms.summary: A gear with only a few teeth drives a full gear part of each turn; between bursts a locking rim holds the driven gear still.

ratio.typical: 90° per driver turn (5 of 20 teeth), dwell 270°

topology.notes: ground, driver with 4 teeth and a convex locking rim, driven gear with 4 concave locking arcs, all in one plane; the gear mesh and the locking contact alternate. The mobility counted from kin is 0 because both contacts are declared; only one acts at a time, so the true mobility is 1.

explain.motion: The driver has teeth on only part of its rim; the rest of its rim is a plain convex locking arc. While the teeth are in mesh, the driven gear turns at the normal gear ratio, the other way. When they have passed, the locking arc slides in a concave arc cut across the tips of two driven teeth and holds the driven gear still. Teeth and lock work in one plane. Here 4 teeth on a 20-tooth pitch carry the driven gear five teeth, 90°, per driver turn, and it rests for the other 270°.
explain.forces: During mesh it acts like an ordinary spur pair at a 20° pressure angle. The first tooth hits the driven gear at full pitch-line speed, so there is a shock at engagement that grows with speed.
explain.benefits: Any step size and dwell split can be set by tooth count, and the driven gear is positively located throughout.
explain.limits: Sudden start and stop cause impact, so it suits slow or light duty. Geneva or cam indexers are preferred at high speed or load.

mechanisms.name: Maccabee eight-night indexer
mechanisms.summary: An eight-slot Geneva steps a rack carriage once a night, carrying the shamash along eight fixed candles; each flame flips up as the shamash reaches it.

ratio.typical: 45° of wheel and 20.03 mm of carriage per driver turn; 140.2 mm from the first night to the eighth

topology.notes: ground with the menorah and the back plate, the driver with its locking disc and pin, the Geneva wheel and its pinion keyed on one shaft, the carriage with its rack and lug, the shamash's slider on the menorah's rail, the six pulleys of the steel tape that joins them, and eight flames, each on a hinge at its candle's wick. The pin in the wheel's slots and the locking disc in its arcs alternate; the pinion meshes the rack; the tape's eight runs tie the slider to the carriage through the pulleys; the finger on the shamash's slider meets each flame's lever (a trip contact), and a toggle spring holds each flame up or folded. The mobility counted from kin is not the true one: the pinion is a body of its own keyed on the wheel's shaft, the contacts each count only while engaged, and each flame rests on its toggle spring between trips; the true mobility is 1.

explain.motion: A driver turning once per day carries a pin that enters one of the wheel's eight radial slots, turns the wheel 45° and leaves. For the rest of the turn a locking disc on the driver sits in a concave arc on the wheel and holds it still. A 34-tooth pinion on the wheel shaft drives a rack under the menorah, and a steel tape looped through the menorah's hollow stems and bar makes the shamash, on a slider in front of the row of eight fixed candles, follow the rack's carriage exactly: every index moves it 20.03 mm, one candle to the left. As the shamash arrives, a finger on its slider tips that candle's flame up from where it lies folded back, and a toggle spring holds it up. Night by night the menorah fills from right to left, in keeping with the custom of placing candles from the right.
explain.forces: Load passes from pin to slot flank, and the wheel is accelerated from rest at entry and stopped at exit, with the peak wheel speed at mid-index (0.62 times driver speed for eight slots). At one turn per day these inertial effects are negligible: the carriage averages 0.62 µm/s while indexing, about 130 times the speed of beard growth, which is the comparison clients ask for. The flame's trip takes a few grams at the finger and comes in the last part of the index, when the carriage is slowing. In the dwell the locking arc carries any load on the carriage straight to ground, so pushing the shamash does nothing, by design.
explain.benefits: Exact, repeatable steps with a positive lock between them and no controller, from one motor running continuously. The index is phased away from the evening, so the shamash is always at rest when the candles are lit, and the flames keep the count of the nights without being asked.
explain.limits: Each index occupies 135° of the driver, nine hours at one turn per day, and must be phased to fall between 01:00 and 10:00. After the eighth night the drive is switched off and the carriage returned by lifting the rack out of mesh, a once-a-year operation; a reset tab on the shamash's slider folds the flames down as it passes them on the way back. Candle pitch is fixed at 20.03 mm by the pinion; standard candles fit, but the spacing is not adjustable without changing the pinion, and the Municipal variant uses a 1:12 rack lever to reach street-scale spacing.

build.ground: the base, the carved plinth with the see-through back plate standing on it, the rails under the wheel, and the menorah: two stems, the bar, eight turned cups and their candles
build.defining_relations: r = c sin(π/n) = 22.96 mm and R = c cos(π/n) = 55.43 mm with n = 8 and c = 60 mm; the pin enters each slot radially, so there is no impact along the slot. Index angle 2π/n = 45°; drive angle during index π − 2π/n = 135°, dwell 225°. Carriage step = (2π/n) × m z / 2 = 20.03 mm with z = 34 and m = 1.5 mm. Peak wheel to driver speed ratio r/(c − r) = 0.62. Flame k turns up as the carriage reaches station k: the finger meets its lever in the last 6 mm of the index and tips it past centre, and the toggle spring holds it.
build.notes: Wheel centre W at the origin, driver centre D 60 mm to its right; the rack's pitch line 25.5 mm under the wheel, the carriage on two rails; the cups' tops 92 mm above W, station k at x = 62 − 20.03 (k − 1), night 1 at the right. The stage cycle is eight driver turns, the eight nights, from the first night's evening: the driver's 0 is mid-dwell with the pin pointing away from the wheel, and each index falls in the middle of a turn (112.5° to 247.5°). Seven indexes move the carriage in mesh; the eighth is the yearly return, compressed into the cycle: the rack out of mesh, the carriage carried back 140.2 mm to the first station in step with that index, and a reset tab on the shamash's slider, 10 mm ahead of the shamash, folding flames 8 to 2 as it passes them. The first flame stays up. The shamash stands on a slider on a brass rail under the bar's front, 12 mm above the candles and set forward of the row; a drop on its pan carries the finger and the tab beside the flames. A closed steel tape 2.5 x 0.3 on six pulleys Ø2.4 runs the slider with the carriage: from a lug on the carriage, down behind the wheel into the plinth, round a turnaround at the right, back under the lug to the left stem's foot, up the hollow stem, over a pulley in the bar's left end, along a channel in the bar's foot where the slider's tongue is clamped to it, over a pulley in the bar's right end, down the right stem, round its foot and back over the lug to a turnaround at the left and the lug. The wheel's and the driver's shafts are held by the back plate; the carriage runs on a way and a keeper lip on it. Each flame's lever stands 4.5 mm beside its candle, under the finger's ramp. Range: driver 360° a night; wheel 45° a night; carriage 7 steps, 140.2 mm; flames 0 to 90°, one more each night.

review.note: T2 review 2026-11-05 on the record, from the solved motion at the first night's evening, mid-index, the end of the first index, the fourth night, the eighth night and the yearly return: tweak. The principle is the eight-slot Geneva and the rack it steps: the pin is traced with the comet, the line of centres and the slot line are drawn, and the 135 degree drive window is marked on the pin's circle; the plot gives the carriage's travel against the driver over the eight nights, a staircase of seven steps with long flats, with the flames up as a second line. Decisions: the stage cycle is eight driver turns, the eight nights, opening on the first night's evening with the shamash over the first candle and its flame up. Seven indexes move the carriage in mesh, one station a night to the left, and the finger on the shamash's slider tips each flame over centre in the last 6 mm of its index. The eighth index closes the cycle as the yearly return, compressed into it: the rack is out of mesh, the carriage is carried back 140.2 mm to the first station in step with that index, and a reset tab on the shamash's slider, ahead of the shamash, folds flames 8 to 2 as it passes them going back; the first flame, where the shamash stops, stays up. In the real menorah the drive is off for the return and it is made by hand. The reset is a tab on the slider rather than a separate reset bar under the bar: it needs no motion of its own and folds each flame as the shamash passes it, and it never meets a flame on the way out, since the flames up all lie behind the shamash. A time map slows each index four times, so the step and the trip can be followed. The shamash rides the menorah itself, on a slider on a rail under the bar's front, raised above the row and set forward of it; nothing of the drive crosses over the candles. A closed steel tape, as a drafting machine's cable loop, runs it exactly with the carriage, both ways: from the carriage's lug in the plinth round two turnarounds, up the hollow left stem, over a pulley in the bar's end, along the bar's channel past the slider, down the right stem and back. A plain loop would run its top against its bottom; the two turnarounds make the top run go the carriage's way. The tape is mostly hidden (an exception): slots in the stems and along the bar's foot show it. mechanisms.name: Internal Geneva drive
mechanisms.summary: A crank pin works inside a cup-shaped slotted wheel, stepping it the same way as the crank with a longer, gentler move and shorter dwell.

ratio.typical: 90° per index (4-slot), moving for 270° of crank, dwell 90°

topology.notes: ground, crank with pin and locking cam, internal slotted wheel; pin-in-slot and locking contact alternate, so only one acts at a time; counted mobility 0 with both declared

explain.motion: The slotted wheel is a cup with slots pointing inward from its rim; the crank sits inside the cup with its axis offset from the wheel axis. The pin enters a slot tangentially and drives the wheel the same way as the crank for 270° of crank rotation, then a locking cam on the crank holds the wheel for the remaining 90°.
explain.forces: Since the move is spread over a longer crank angle, peak angular acceleration is much lower than in an external Geneva of the same slot count. The crank must be overhung (supported on one side only) because the wheel surrounds it.
explain.benefits: Smoother motion with lower peak acceleration, same-direction rotation and a compact package.
explain.limits: Dwell is short (less than half the cycle), and the overhung crank limits load. Hard to make with few slots because the pin path must fit inside the cup.

mechanisms.name: Roller gear cam indexer
mechanisms.summary: A tapered rib cam on a constantly turning shaft steps a turret of rollers by one station, then locks it between the ribs.

ratio.typical: 45° per index (8 stops), index in 120° of camshaft, dwell 240°

topology.notes: ground, globoidal cam shaft, turret with radial rollers; two rollers in contact with the rib at all times (preloaded), so the pair is overconstrained on purpose: counted mobility 0, the two contacts hold one motion

explain.motion: The input camshaft turns at constant speed. A raised rib wraps part way round a waisted (globoidal) cam; in its straight section it holds two turret rollers and the turret dwells, and in its twisted section it pushes the rollers along, rotating the turret one station. One cam turn gives one index.
explain.forces: Rollers are preloaded against both rib flanks, so there is no backlash and the turret is locked during dwell. Torque passes through rolling contact, and the cam law (modified sine) keeps peak acceleration and jerk low.
explain.benefits: High precision, high speed and no backlash, with smooth motion set by the cam law. Very rigid locking in dwell.
explain.limits: Expensive to make, fixed stop count and index time once cut, and needs a clutch or brake for overload. Bulky compared with a Geneva for light loads.

mechanisms.name: Barrel cam
mechanisms.summary: A helical groove around a rotating drum pushes a roller follower back and forth parallel to the drum axis.

ratio.typical: stroke = groove axial travel (30 mm by default) per drum turn

topology.notes: ground, drum, follower slide, roller; roller in groove is a form-closed cam contact; counted mobility 2, because the roller's spin about its pin is a passive extra freedom

explain.motion: A groove cut around the drum surface wanders along the axis. A roller sitting in the groove is carried with it, so the follower slide moves parallel to the drum axis as the drum turns. The default groove rises 30 mm over 120°, dwells 60°, returns over 120° and dwells 60°.
explain.forces: Groove walls push both ways, so no return spring is needed. The pressure angle is set by groove slope: tan(phi) = s'/Rp, where Rp is the pitch radius; a larger drum gives a gentler slope and lower side load. In this default, here Rp is 60 mm and phi peaks at 25.5°.
explain.benefits: Positive (form-closed) motion along the shaft axis, compact for long strokes, and can hold several followers on one drum.
explain.limits: Groove backlash means the roller flips walls at reversals, causing wear and noise. Machining a 3D groove is costlier than a plate cam.

mechanisms.name: Cam and roller follower
mechanisms.summary: A shaped disc lifts a roller follower along its guide, so the output motion is whatever profile you cut into the cam.

ratio.typical: stroke = rise h (22 mm by default) per cam turn, with 60° dwells at the top and the bottom

topology.notes: ground, cam, follower stem, roller; cam contact is the higher pair; counted mobility 2, because the roller's spin about its pin is a passive extra freedom

explain.motion: As the cam turns, the roller rides its edge and the follower rises and falls along its guide. In this default the follower rises 22 mm over 120° of cam turn, dwells at the top for 60°, returns over 120° and dwells at the bottom for 60°, with the cycloidal law on the rise and the return. The cam is the displacement diagram wrapped round its base circle, so any timing can be drawn into the outline.
explain.forces: The cam can only push along the contact normal through the roller centre. The pressure angle between that normal and the follower path decides how much of the push goes sideways into the guide. Here it peaks at 23.6°, part way up the rise and part way down the return; keep it under about 30°. A spring or gravity must hold the follower on the cam.
explain.benefits: Almost any motion law with two moving parts and exact timing. A roller turns sliding into rolling contact, cutting wear.
explain.limits: Needs a return spring, which can float at high speed. Large lift in a short angle forces a big cam or high pressure angles.

mechanisms.name: Cam with flat-faced follower
mechanisms.summary: A disc cam pushes a follower with a flat face, so contact slides across the face and the push always stays square to the stroke.

ratio.typical: stroke = rise h (15 mm by default) per cam turn

topology.notes: ground, cam, flat-faced follower; cam contact slides along the face

explain.motion: The cam turns and its lobe pushes the flat face of the follower up its guide. The contact point slides sideways across the face by a distance equal to ds/dtheta. The default profile rises cycloidally over 120°, dwells 60°, returns over 120° and dwells 60°.
explain.forces: The contact normal is always perpendicular to the face, so the pressure angle is zero for an in-line follower and guide side load comes only from friction and contact offset. The sliding contact carries high Hertz stress and needs good lubrication.
explain.benefits: Very compact and stiff with no side thrust from pressure angle, which suits direct-acting engine valves.
explain.limits: The cam must be convex everywhere (no concave flanks), and the face must be wide enough for the contact excursion. Sliding friction causes wear, so flat tappets need careful break-in.

mechanisms.name: Face groove cam
mechanisms.summary: A roller runs in a closed groove cut into the face of a disc, so the cam drives the follower both out and back without a spring.

ratio.typical: stroke = rise h (20 mm by default) per cam turn

topology.notes: ground, grooved disc, radial follower slide, roller; groove gives form-closed cam contact; counted mobility 2, because the roller's spin about its pin is a passive extra freedom

explain.motion: The groove is a closed loop machined into the face of the disc; its distance from the centre varies with angle. The roller sits in the groove, so as the disc turns the follower is pulled in and pushed out along its radial guide. The default track rises over 120°, dwells 60°, returns over 120° and dwells 60° with a 3-4-5 polynomial law.
explain.forces: Either groove wall can push, so the follower is driven in both directions and cannot float. Pressure angle limits are the same as a plate cam; the roller reverses which wall it touches when acceleration changes sign.
explain.benefits: Positive motion with no return spring, so it works at high speed and in any orientation.
explain.limits: Roller wall-switching causes backlash, noise and wear, and the roller spins the wrong way when it touches the outer wall. A wider, heavier disc than a plate cam.

mechanisms.name: Desmodromic valve cam
mechanisms.summary: Two matched cams and rockers open and close a valve mechanically, so the valve follows the cam with no return spring.

ratio.typical: lift 12 mm per cam turn: rise 90°, return 90°, closed 180°

topology.notes: ground, camshaft (opening and closing lobes), opening rocker, closing rocker, follower; cam-rocker and rocker-follower contacts; overconstrained on purpose (conjugate cams): counted mobility 0, the four contacts hold one motion

explain.motion: An opening lobe pushes the opening rocker down onto the valve stem, opening the valve. A second, conjugate closing lobe drives a forked closing rocker that pulls up on a collar on the valve stem, closing it. The two profiles are cut so that at every angle one rocker or the other holds the valve, so lift follows the law exactly.
explain.forces: The opening cam carries gas and inertia loads on opening; the closing cam carries the inertia of deceleration and the closing pull that a spring would normally supply. Rocker sliding contacts carry high loads and need tight clearance control.
explain.benefits: No valve float at high revs and no spring force to overcome, so aggressive lift laws are possible.
explain.limits: Two clearances per valve to set, more parts and sliding friction, and conjugate profiles must be ground very accurately. Modern valve springs and pneumatic returns reduce its advantage.

mechanisms.name: Hobson's joint
mechanisms.summary: Rods bent at a right angle slide in bores of two discs on shafts at 90°, so the output turns exactly with the input, with no gears.

ratio.typical: 1:1 exactly at every instant, round the fixed angle the rods are bent to (90° here)

topology.notes: ground, input and output discs on their revolutes, three bent rods each held by two cylindrical joints (one leg in a bore of each disc); counted mobility -4: the joint is overconstrained, since the count does not see that every leg is held parallel to its shaft and that all the bores lie on one radius; it moves with 1 degree of freedom

explain.motion: Each shaft ends in a disc with three bores on a 22 mm circle, the same in both. Three rods bent at 90° pass through the bores, one leg in each disc, each leg parallel to its own shaft. A leg can only slide and turn in its bore, so a rod never turns: it is carried round, its corner keeping to the plane that bisects the right angle, and the two discs are held at the same angle. The output turns at exactly the input's speed at every instant, and each leg slides 44 mm out and back in its bore on every turn.
explain.forces: Torque passes as the push of each leg on the side of its bore, 22 mm from each axis, and the rods carry it round the corner in bending. The legs slide in their bores while they carry the load, so the sliding friction is the joint's loss.
explain.benefits: Constant velocity round a right angle with no gears and no cross: two drilled discs and a few bent rods, and it drives either way.
explain.limits: The shaft angle is fixed by the bend of the rods and cannot change. The legs slide under load, so the joint binds when the bores are not true, wears in its bores and suits low speeds and light torque. One rod, or two set opposite each other, would not do: twice a turn it can carry the output on backwards, so three or more are spaced round the circle.

build.ground: base with two pillow blocks under each shaft, the shafts level and at a right angle, their axes meeting at J
build.defining_relations: Bores on one radius r = 22 mm in both discs; rods bent to the shafts' angle beta = 90°. A rod's corner B lies on its input bore line and r from the output axis. With B - J = x a1 + q (q square to the input axis a1), x = (q · a2) / (1 - cos beta) on the assembled root, so at 90° x = q · a2: the corners keep to the plane through J that bisects the right angle, and output angle = input angle exactly. Each leg slides r cos(theta) from mid-stroke, a stroke of 2r = 44 mm per turn. The other root, x = -(q · a2) / (1 + cos beta), turns the output the other way; it meets the assembled one where q · a2 = 0 (the rod's bores straight above or below the shafts), twice a turn for each rod. Rods at 0°, 120° and 240° reach those points one at a time, so the other two hold the output on its root.
build.notes: Shafts level at 55 mm, the input along x and the output along y, their axes meeting at J; discs Ø64 x 12 with their front faces 56 mm from J; rods Ø6 with 94 mm legs and a 6 mm bend radius, the bores through, so each leg's end comes out behind its disc as it slides. The rod count is a design choice: three is the fewest rods spaced evenly round the circle that keep the output on its root through every point (two set opposite reach their switch points together). The reference has rod 1 in the plane of the shafts, its corner at the outer end of its stroke.

review.note: New record, reviewed against its kinematics before the build (#256). Six phases of the solved cycle (input 0, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300): rod 1's corner runs (22, 22, 0), (11, 11, 19), (-11, -11, 19), (-22, -22, 0), (-11, -11, -19), (11, 11, -19) from J, an ellipse in the plane x = y that bisects the right angle; the rods never turn; each leg slides 44 mm in its bore, the corner farthest from both discs at 0 and nearest at 180, both legs of a rod together; speed ratio 1 within 1e-4, output minus input 0, K1 residual 1e-14. Branch: the other root of a rod's corner (x = -q · a2) turns the output the other way and meets the assembled root where the rod's bores stand straight above or below the shafts (input 90 and 270 for rod 1); solved for all three rods, the other root gives each rod a different output turn, so it cannot be taken while the other two hold the output, and the rods reach their switch points one at a time, 60 degrees apart. Two rods set opposite would reach theirs together and could not hold it, so three rods at 120 degrees. Decided: bores on a 22 mm circle in Ø64 discs 36 mm from J, a stroke large enough to see against the disc; the reference with rod 1 in the plane of the shafts, so the section in that plane cuts both its legs along their bores. What must be seen: equal angles on both shafts, by a mark on each disc's face at the same angle traced with ticks every 30 degrees (the same twelve ticks on both); rod 1's corner traced with the comet; the corners' plane as a line; the leg stroke as a dimension between its posed ends; why the angle is fixed, by the shaft angle arc beside the rod's bend arc, both 90 degrees. Both discs see-through on purpose (teaching.seeThrough) so the legs show in their bores. Default view VIEW 135 30. Controls: the input only; the shaft angle is fixed by the bend of the rods, so it is not offered. Looked at again on the finished build (record view, PLAN, SIDE, the 28° view, the section and the explode, both sheets): keep. The view from the outside corner of the right angle replaced ISOMETRIC, where the output disc stood in front of the rods' corners; there both discs face the viewer at 45° with their arrows and ticks side by side and the three bends in front; the corner's trace lies edge-on in it (its plane holds the line of sight) and reads in SIDE and the 28° view. mechanisms.name: Locomotive driving gear
mechanisms.summary: A piston, crosshead and main rod turn one driving wheel, and a coupling rod makes the next wheel turn exactly with it.

ratio.typical: stroke = 2 x crank radius (34 mm); coupled wheels turn 1:1

topology.notes: crosshead, main rod, two wheels, coupling rod, ground; the coupling loop is a parallelogram four-bar; count includes ground

explain.motion: Steam pushes the piston back and forth. The crosshead, sliding between guide bars, carries the piston rod and turns that push into the swinging main rod, which drives the crank pin on the main wheel. The coupling rod joins crank pins set at the same angle on both wheels, so it stays level, every point on it circles at crank radius, and the wheels turn together.
explain.forces: The crosshead takes the side thrust of the tilted main rod so the piston does not. Torque falls to zero at each dead centre, so real locomotives set the cranks on the two sides 90° apart (quartered) to always have one side able to start.
explain.benefits: Spreads tractive effort over several wheels for grip, with a simple, robust and inspectable rod drive.
explain.limits: Rods and counterweights cause hammer blow and shaking that pound the track. Each side alone has dead centres, and the parallelogram has change points where a slack rod could jam.

mechanisms.name: Oldham coupling
mechanisms.summary: Two parallel offset shafts joined by a floating disc with crossed tongues; the output turns at exactly input speed while the disc centre circles twice per turn.

ratio.typical: exactly 1:1 at every instant; disc centre orbits at 2x shaft speed on a circle of diameter e

topology.notes: ground, input hub, floating disc (with both tongues), output hub; two prismatic tongue-in-slot pairs at right angles; a double-slider (elliptic trammel inversion)

explain.motion: Each shaft carries a hub with a straight slot across its face. The middle disc has two tongues at right angles, one on each face, and each tongue slides in one hub's slot. Because the tongues are square to each other, both hubs must turn through the same angle, and the disc's centre runs round a small circle between the two shaft centres, twice for every turn of the shafts.
explain.forces: Torque passes as side forces between the tongues and the walls of the slots, square to each slot. The offset itself puts little bending on the shafts, but the tongues slide back and forth once per turn, so the faces need lubrication or a low-friction disc and wear grows with offset and speed.
explain.benefits: The speed ratio is exactly one at every instant, unlike a single universal joint. It takes up parallel offset in a short length, and the middle disc can be a cheap plastic part that also insulates and acts as a torque fuse.
explain.limits: Only small offsets in practice (a few percent of diameter) because sliding wear and the orbiting disc's unbalance grow with offset. Little angular misalignment capacity and some backlash unless spring-loaded.

mechanisms.name: Universal joint
mechanisms.summary: Two yokes joined by a cross let shafts at an angle drive each other, but the output speed speeds up and slows down twice per turn.

ratio.typical: 1:1 on average; instantaneous ratio swings between cos(beta) and 1/cos(beta), 0.866 to 1.155 at 30°

topology.notes: ground, input yoke, cross (spider), output yoke; a spherical 4R chain with all four axes meeting at the cross centre. Overconstrained in the joint count: Kutzbach gives -2 because it ignores that the four axes are concurrent; the true mobility is 1, solved in closed form by the Hooke block.

explain.motion: Each shaft ends in a fork (yoke), and the two forks are joined by a cross whose arms run in bearings in the forks. As the input turns, the cross wobbles so the output yoke follows round at an angle. Over a full turn both shafts turn 360°, but within the turn the output runs ahead and then behind, twice per revolution.
explain.forces: Torque passes through the cross arms as forces in the yoke bearings. The speed fluctuation causes angular acceleration of the output and its inertia, giving torque ripple and vibration that grows sharply with angle; the yokes also feel a secondary bending couple.
explain.benefits: Simple, strong and compact, it carries large torque across angles of up to about 30° to 45° and is cheap to make with needle-bearing crosses.
explain.limits: Not constant velocity: at 30° the output speed varies by about ±15%. Above about 45° it locks up, and it needs pairs (double cardan or phased driveshaft) to cancel the fluctuation.

mechanisms.name: Double Cardan joint
mechanisms.summary: Two universal joints back to back with a short centre yoke cancel each other's speed wobble, giving constant velocity across an angle.

ratio.typical: exactly 1:1 when both joint angles are equal and the centre yokes are in phase

topology.notes: ground, input yoke, cross 1, centre yoke, cross 2, output yoke; 2 shaft bearings plus 2 cross bearings per joint. Overconstrained in the joint count: Kutzbach gives 0 because it ignores that the axes at each cross meet at its centre (two spherical chains); the true mobility is 1, solved in closed form by two Hooke blocks. A ball-and-socket centring device (spherical pair, not counted) keeps the two joint angles equal.

explain.motion: The input yoke drives a first cross, which drives a short centre yoke, which drives a second cross and the output yoke. Each single joint makes the speed fluctuate, but because the two joints are set at equal angles with the centre yoke forks in the same plane, the second joint's speed-up exactly cancels the first one's slow-down. A centring ball and socket between the two shafts keeps the two angles equal as the total angle changes.
explain.forces: Torque passes through both crosses, each carrying it as yoke-bearing forces; the centre yoke still accelerates twice per turn, but the output does not. The centring device carries the small forces that keep the joint angles equal.
explain.benefits: Constant velocity at larger angles than a single U-joint can tolerate, using rugged, serviceable cross-and-bearing parts.
explain.limits: Longer, heavier and more complex than a single joint; constant velocity only holds when the two angles stay equal, and the centring ball wears.

mechanisms.name: Rzeppa CV joint
mechanisms.summary: Six balls held in a cage between grooved inner and outer races stay in the plane bisecting the shaft angle, so the output turns at constant speed.

ratio.typical: exactly 1:1 up to about 45° to 48° joint angle

topology.notes: ground, inner race with shaft, outer race (bell) with shaft, cage, 6 balls; each ball contacts an inner groove, an outer groove and a cage window (18 higher pairs); cage to races are spherical sliding fits. The joint count (Kutzbach, 20) is not the mobility: each ball contact is counted as a point contact, while the groove holds the ball centre on a line, and each ball's spin is an idle freedom; the six balls with the two spherical fits overconstrain the cage. The true mobility is 1, solved in closed form by the homokinetic block.

explain.motion: The inner race on one shaft and the bell-shaped outer race on the other each have six curved grooves. Six balls sit in pairs of facing grooves and in windows of a cage that lies between the races. The groove shapes force the balls, and so the cage, to stay in the plane that bisects the angle between the shafts, which makes the joint symmetric and the two shafts turn at exactly the same speed.
explain.forces: Torque passes from inner race to balls to outer race as contact forces at the groove flanks; the cage only positions the balls. Load is shared between six balls, so it is compact for its torque, but contact stresses are high and need clean grease.
explain.benefits: True constant velocity at large angles in a compact package, ideal for steered driven wheels.
explain.limits: Needs a sealed boot full of grease; a torn boot lets in grit and it fails by clicking and wear. Fixed-type joints do not plunge, so a sliding (tripod or plunging) joint is needed at the other end of the shaft.

mechanisms.name: Schmidt coupling
mechanisms.summary: Three discs joined by sets of parallel links connect widely offset parallel shafts at exactly the same speed, with no side load.

ratio.typical: exactly 1:1 for any offset from near zero up to 2 x link length

topology.notes: ground, input disc, middle disc, output disc, 3 links between input and middle, 3 links between middle and output; 12 link-end pins plus 2 shaft bearings; overconstrained parallelogram sets (3 links where 2 would do, to pass dead centres)

explain.motion: The input disc is linked to a middle disc by three equal links whose pins sit on equal pitch circles 120° apart, and the middle disc is linked the same way to the output disc. Each set of links forms parallelograms, so the joined discs always keep the same orientation: all three discs turn at the same angle. The links themselves do not rotate; they only translate in circles, while the middle disc spins about a fixed point set by the offset.
explain.forces: Torque passes through the links in tension and compression, with the three links of each set sharing load so no set ever sits at a dead centre. Because the parallelograms leave no reaction at the shafts, there is no side load on the bearings from the offset.
explain.benefits: Exact constant velocity with large parallel offsets, and the offset can even change while running. Compact axially compared with a cardan shaft.
explain.limits: Many pins and bearings make it costlier and heavier than an Oldham or bellows coupling. Near zero offset the middle disc position becomes undetermined, so a small minimum offset or support is needed, and it takes little angular misalignment.

mechanisms.name: Lead screw
mechanisms.summary: A threaded shaft turning in a nut that is kept from rotating moves the nut along the shaft by one lead per turn, giving slow, strong linear motion.

ratio.typical: travel = lead per turn, e.g. 3 mm per turn (Tr12x3); leads from under 1 mm to 50 mm

topology.notes: ground, screw (revolute in end bearings), nut (prismatic on a guide); screw to nut is a helical (screw) pair. Overconstrained: the bearings, the guide and the thread share one axis, so the joint count gives -3 while the mechanism moves with 1; the coaxial pairs are redundant, not locking

explain.motion: The screw turns in bearings at its ends while the nut is held by a guide so it cannot spin. Each turn of the screw slides the nut along the axis by one lead, the pitch times the number of starts. Reversing the screw reverses the nut.
explain.forces: The thread is an inclined plane wrapped round a cylinder, so a small torque gives a large axial thrust: ideal thrust F = 2 pi T / lead. Sliding friction on the flanks eats much of this, giving efficiencies of about 20% to 80%, and with small lead angles the friction angle exceeds the lead angle so the load cannot drive the screw back.
explain.benefits: Cheap, quiet, compact and holds its position without a brake when self-locking. Takes high loads and suits manual drives.
explain.limits: Low efficiency means heat and wear, so not for continuous high-speed duty. Backlash grows as the nut wears, and long slender screws whip at high speed (critical speed).

mechanisms.name: Ball screw
mechanisms.summary: A screw and nut with a stream of recirculating steel balls rolling between their grooves, turning rotation into precise, efficient linear motion.

ratio.typical: travel = lead per turn, commonly 5 to 12.7 mm per turn (16x5 default = 5 mm per turn)

topology.notes: ground, screw, nut; the ball train is a rolling screw pair, its balls carried round the circuit and not separate kinematic links. Overconstrained: the bearings, the guide and the ball screw share one axis, so the joint count gives -3 while the mechanism moves with 1

explain.motion: Steel balls sit in matching helical grooves on the screw and inside the nut. As the screw turns, the balls roll along the groove and carry the nut axially by one lead per turn. At the end of the circuit a return tube, internal button or end cap lifts the balls out and feeds them back to the start, so they circulate endlessly.
explain.forces: Load passes through many rolling ball contacts instead of sliding flanks, so efficiency is around 90% and thrust is nearly 2 pi T / lead. Because it is so efficient, an axial load can spin the screw backwards, so vertical axes need a brake.
explain.benefits: High efficiency, long life, low heat and, with a preloaded double nut, zero backlash and high stiffness for precise positioning.
explain.limits: Not self-locking, more expensive than a lead screw, and sensitive to dirt and side load. Long screws are limited by critical speed and buckling.

mechanisms.name: Differential screw
mechanisms.summary: One shaft with two threads of slightly different pitch moves a nut by only the pitch difference per turn, giving very fine adjustment.

ratio.typical: travel = p1 - p2 per turn: 5 - 4 = 1 mm per turn here; fine instrument pairs such as 1.0 - 0.8 = 0.2 mm per turn

topology.notes: ground with fixed nut, screw with two threads, sliding nut on a guide; two screw (helical) pairs plus one prismatic guide. Overconstrained: the two threads and the guide share one axis, so the joint count gives -3 while the mechanism moves with 1

explain.motion: The screw carries two threads of the same hand but different pitch. One thread runs in a nut fixed to the frame, so each turn moves the screw itself forward by p1. The other thread carries a nut that is guided so it cannot turn; relative to the screw it moves back by p2, so its net motion is p1 - p2 per turn.
explain.forces: The effective lead is tiny, so the ideal force ratio is huge: F = 2 pi T / (p1 - p2). In practice friction in two thread pairs makes it strongly self-locking and fairly inefficient.
explain.benefits: Gives very fine motion with coarse, strong, easy-to-make threads instead of one very fine, fragile thread.
explain.limits: Low efficiency and slow travel, and backlash in two thread pairs adds up. Total stroke is limited by the length of the threads.

mechanisms.name: Self-reversing screw
mechanisms.summary: A screw cut with a right-hand and a left-hand groove joined at the ends drives a shoe to and fro at constant speed while it turns one way.

ratio.typical: one lead per turn (48 mm by default); stroke = lead x (turns per traverse - turn-round), 120 mm over 3 turns

topology.notes: ground, screw (revolute in its pillow blocks), carriage (prismatic on its guide), shoe (revolute pivot in the carriage); the shoe in the groove is a form-closed cam contact; counted mobility 2, because the shoe's swivel on its pivot is set by the groove's walls, which the count does not see

explain.motion: The screw carries a right-hand and a left-hand groove of the same lead, joined at both ends into one endless track that crosses itself twice on every turn. A shoe rides the groove on a pivot in the carriage. Turning the screw one way at a steady speed carries the shoe along at a steady 48 mm per turn. Near each end the groove bends round within 1 turn of the screw: the shoe slows, stops, swivels across into the other groove and comes back, so the carriage runs 120 mm there and back every 6 turns with the screw never changing direction.
explain.forces: The groove's wall pushes on the side of the shoe, and the push along the screw is the turning effort over the lead, less friction. At the pitch radius the grooves lean 28.6° from the circumference, so the shoe swivels through 57.2° at each turn-round. Where the grooves cross, the shoe loses its walls in the middle and is carried by its two ends, which is why it must be longer than a crossing.
explain.benefits: Turns steady one-way rotation into a steady to-and-fro with no reversing gear, clutch or change of direction, and the reversal points are cut into the screw, so they never drift.
explain.limits: The stroke and the reversal points are fixed when the screw is cut. The sharp points where the grooves cross and the long shoe wear fastest, and a worn shoe can turn into the wrong groove and reverse early; heavy loads wear the shoe quickly.

build.ground: base with the screw's two pillow blocks and a straight guide for the carriage along the screw
build.defining_relations: Both grooves have the lead p = 48 mm; at the pitch radius rp = 14 mm the lead angle is atan(p / (2 pi rp)) = 28.6°. Over each traverse of N = 3 turns the shoe moves by the trapezoidal law: steady at one lead per turn, with a parabolic turn-round of tr = 0.5 turn at each end (blend tr / N = 1/6), so the stroke is h = p (N - tr) = 120 mm and the track repeats after 2N = 6 turns. The shoe lies along the groove: its swivel is the change of atan(s' / rp), plus or minus 28.6° in the steady runs. Groove 7 mm wide and 4 mm deep; at the lead angle a crossing is 7 / sin(57.2°) = 8.3 mm long along the groove, bridged by a shoe 18 mm long.
build.notes: Screw axis horizontal, the shoe on the near side, seen in front elevation where the grooves cross in a diamond pattern. The track is cut by Manifold in pieces along the law, the root turned back as one core. The shoe's blade is an ellipse in plan, its underside cut round the screw's axis; it swivels on a pivot bolt in the carriage's upright.

review.note: New record, reviewed against its kinematics before the build (#255). Six phases of the solved cycle (every 60 degrees of the cycle, one turn of the screw): the shoe at mid-stroke on a crossing, 48 mm further, at the far end turning round (swivel through 0 to -57.2), and back the same way; the shoe's travel against the screw's turn is an exact triangle wave with rounded tips, 24 mm per half turn in the steady runs. Decided: 3 turns per traverse and a turn-round of half a turn either side of each end, so the cycle is 6 turns, the shoe runs steady for 2 of every 3 turns and the turn-round is a sixth of the cycle, long enough to watch with no time map; lead 48 on a 32 mm screw, a lead angle of 28.6 degrees at the 14 mm pitch radius, so a crossing is 8.3 mm long and an 18 mm shoe bridges it with 4.8 mm in the groove at each end; the reference at mid-stroke, where both grooves cross under the shoe, so the opening drawing shows the shoe bridging a crossing. Default view DIMETRIC (owner's review): the screw's length, the diamonds of the crossing grooves and the shoe in its groove read together with the depth of the carriage and drive; FRONT keeps the grooves at true size. One tick per screw turn on the shoe's trace, a fixed one-lead dimension above it and the stroke dimension between the posed ends, so a turn reads as one lead; plot of the shoe's position against the screw's turn (the triangle wave over 6 turns); a detail view at the crossing under the shoe at the reference. The carriage is drawn see-through on purpose (teaching.seeThrough): its upright stands in front of the shoe in FRONT. Controls: the screw's turn only; the lead, turns and turn-round are built into the screw, so they are not offered. 30 Oct 2026 (#273): the part to watch is the shoe, small in its groove under the carriage, tinted in the accent keeping its see-through (T18); reviewed by the owner on the stage: keep.

mechanisms.name: Belt drive
mechanisms.summary: A tensioned loop of belt wrapped round two pulleys carries rotation between distant shafts, changing speed by the ratio of pulley diameters.

ratio.typical: 1:1 to 6:1 per stage, ratio = D2/D1 (2:1 default)

topology.notes: ground, driving pulley, driven pulley, belt; two belt wraps as higher pairs; an idler/tensioner adds one revolute

explain.motion: Both pulleys are on parallel shafts and a tensioned belt runs round them. With no slip the belt speed is the same at each pulley rim, so the speeds are inversely proportional to the diameters. An open belt turns both pulleys the same way, a crossed belt reverses the output.
explain.forces: Torque is carried by the difference between the tight-side and slack-side tensions, limited by friction over the wrap angle (T1/T2 up to e^(mu theta)). Shaft bearings carry the sum of both tensions; small pulleys with short centre distance reduce wrap and grip.
explain.benefits: Quiet, cheap, tolerant of misalignment, spans long centre distances, needs no lubrication and slips on overload to protect the machine. Toothed timing belts add exact, slip-free timing.
explain.limits: Friction belts creep 0.5% to 1% and can slip, so the ratio is not exact. Belts stretch and age and need tension adjustment; not for very high torque in a small space.

mechanisms.name: Block and tackle
mechanisms.summary: A rope reeved through a fixed and a moving block of pulleys lifts a load with a pull divided by the number of rope parts holding it.

ratio.typical: MA = number of supporting rope parts, 2:1 (gun tackle) to 6:1 (threefold purchase); 4:1 default

topology.notes: ground with fixed block, moving block (vertical guide idealised as prismatic), 4 sheaves on their pins; rope wraps on each sheave as higher pairs; rope is a flexible member

explain.motion: The rope is tied to one block and threaded alternately round the sheaves of the fixed upper block and the moving lower block. Pulling the free end (the fall) shortens every rope part between the blocks equally, so the load rises by the pull distance divided by the number of supporting parts.
explain.forces: Each supporting part carries the same tension, so the hauling force is the load divided by n in the ideal case. Sheave bearing and rope bending friction add a few percent per sheave, so real advantage is lower and too many sheaves can cancel the gain.
explain.benefits: Very simple, light and portable, uses ordinary rope, and the advantage is easy to change by re-reeving.
explain.limits: Long hauling distance for a small lift, friction losses and twisting of the rope. Not self-locking: the load runs back if the fall is released, so a cleat or brake is needed.

mechanisms.name: Chain drive
mechanisms.summary: A roller chain meshing with toothed sprockets carries rotation between parallel shafts with no slip, in the ratio of tooth counts.

ratio.typical: 1:1 to 7:1 per stage, ratio = z2/z1 (30/15 = 2:1 default)

topology.notes: ground, driving sprocket, driven sprocket, chain (treated as one flexible member); two sprocket-chain meshes as higher pairs; each chain link is internally a revolute chain

explain.motion: The chain is a loop of pin-jointed links whose rollers sit between sprocket teeth. As the driver turns, each tooth pulls a roller, the tight span drags the driven sprocket round, and the slack span returns. Speeds are inversely proportional to tooth counts because the same number of links pass each sprocket.
explain.forces: Torque is carried only by the tight span tension; the slack span hangs nearly unloaded. Because the chain wraps as a polygon, the effective radius rises and falls once per tooth (chordal action), causing small speed ripple and impact as each roller seats, worst on small sprockets.
explain.benefits: No slip, high load in a compact width, efficiency up to about 98%, and long centre distances with simple parts. Several shafts can be driven from one chain.
explain.limits: Needs lubrication and protection from dirt, wears and stretches, and is noisier than a belt. Chordal speed variation and vibration limit high-speed use with small sprockets.

mechanisms.name: Belt CVT (variable pulley)
mechanisms.summary: Two V-pulleys with movable cone halves change their working diameters together, so a belt gives a stepless ratio.

ratio.typical: about 0.4:1 to 2.5:1 here (spread about 6.2); car CVTs typically spread 5 to 7

topology.notes: ground, input shaft with fixed sheave, input movable sheave, output shaft with fixed sheave, output movable sheave; the belt joins the two shafts. Movable sheaves slide on splines on opposite sides. Mobility counted from the joints is 3: the input sheave's slide is the ratio setting, a second controlled freedom, and the output sheave's slide follows from the fixed belt length; the drive is one

explain.motion: Each pulley is a pair of cones; one cone can slide along the shaft. Squeezing the input cones together pushes the belt outward to a larger radius, while the output cones spread so the belt sinks inward, which raises the output speed. Because the belt length is fixed, the two radii change together and the ratio moves smoothly between the limits.
explain.forces: Torque is carried by friction between the belt flanks and the sheave cones, so large clamping forces, from springs, flyweights or hydraulics, are needed. A steel push belt transmits by compression between its elements; rubber belts by tension.
explain.benefits: Keeps the engine at its best speed with no shift steps, simple to automate, and smooth.
explain.limits: Torque is limited by clamping force and belt strength, efficiency is a few percent below gears, and belts wear or slip if overloaded.

mechanisms.name: Chain stroke doubler
mechanisms.summary: A chain anchored to the frame runs round a sprocket on a moving carrier to an output slide, which moves twice as far as the carrier.

ratio.typical: output stroke = 2 x carrier stroke for any sprocket; 160 mm for an 80 mm carrier stroke

topology.notes: ground, carrier (prismatic on the ground), sprocket (revolute on the carrier), output (prismatic on the ground); four chain strands, each a higher pair: two chains, each with an anchored strand and a running strand. Overconstrained by two: the second chain repeats the first's relation the other way round, which is why the pair is tensioned against each other at one anchor

explain.motion: A carrier slides back and forth with a sprocket turning free on a stud. A roller chain is anchored to the frame, runs along under the sprocket, round its end and back over it to the output slide. When the carrier moves, the anchored strand grows by the carrier's travel, so the strand on the other side of the sprocket must shrink by the same amount: the chain runs round the sprocket and its far end moves twice as far, the same way. The output moves 160 mm while the carrier moves 80 mm, at twice its speed at every point of the stroke.
explain.forces: The sprocket is the moving pulley of a block and tackle, driven at its centre instead of at the rope: the output's load pulls the running strand, the anchored strand holds the same tension, so the carrier pushes with twice the output force. A chain only pulls, so a second chain round the other side of the sprocket, anchored at the frame's other end, pulls the output back.
explain.benefits: Doubles a stroke with one driven slide and no second drive, positively and exactly, and the doubling holds for any sprocket size, since only the anchored strand sets it.
explain.limits: Each direction needs its own chain, and the two must be kept tight against each other; chain stretch and slack at the anchors show twice at the output. The carrier needs twice the output force, and the ratio cannot be changed.

build.ground: base with the carrier's slide, the output's slide beside it, and an anchor block for each chain's held end, one at either end of the base
build.defining_relations: The sprocket (ISO 606 08B, 12 teeth, seat circle radius 24.53 mm) takes 152.4 mm of chain per turn, so r = z p / 2π = 24.26 mm. Each chain's anchored strand is held: for a carrier travel x the sprocket turns θ = -x / r, and the strand on its far side moves x again relative to the carrier, so the output moves x - r θ = 2x, whatever r is. Carrier stroke 80 mm (±40), output stroke 160 mm (±80), sprocket turn 189° over the stroke (80 / 24.26 rad).
build.notes: Seen in plan: the anchored strands run under the sprocket's centre (y -24.53), the running strands over it (y +24.53), the output slide beyond them. Chain A, in the sprocket's lower row, wraps its +x half: anchored at x -114.3, pinned to the output at -76.2. Chain B, in the upper row 16.5 mm higher, wraps the -x half: anchored at +114.3, pinned to the output at +76.2. Both 21 links, a whole number of pitches from each end to the sprocket, so a roller sits in a seat at both tangent points. Each chain end is pinned to an anchor bolt; the nuts on the bolts set each chain's length, the two chains drawn tight against each other.
